title: Takashi Nagai
hookLine: a Catholic doctor in Nagasaki who kept treating the wounded after the bomb killed his wife

cards: In the ashes of a kitchen, a man kneels and picks up a few blackened bones, and beside them, a melted chain of rosary beads. He knows whose they are.
He is a doctor, a radiologist, and a few days earlier he was at work in his hospital in Nagasaki when the atomic bomb fell. Bleeding from his own wounds, he spent those days treating other people.
Only then did he come home to look for his wife, Midori. He carries what he found back in a bucket.

teach.b: Nagai grew up outside the church and came to Catholic faith as a young man, in Nagasaki's Urakami district, where Christian families had kept their faith in secret through long years of persecution.
His wife Midori came from one of those families.

teach.h: ILL BEFORE THE BOMB, WORKING AFTER.
teach.b: By the time the bomb fell, he was already ill: years of work with X-rays, without much protection, had given him leukemia. The bomb made everything worse.
He set up first aid in the ruins with the staff who were still alive, and worked until he collapsed. His children survived because they had been sent to the countryside.

teach.h: A HUT NAMED FOR LOVE OF NEIGHBOR.
teach.b: Afterward he lived with them in a tiny hut near the ruins of the cathedral, and named it for a line of Jesus. In the King James Bible: "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself."
From his bed, as his illness grew, he wrote books, including one called The Bells of Nagasaki. The title comes from the cathedral.

teach.h: THE BELL DUG OUT OF THE RUBBLE.
teach.b: Its bells had been buried in the rubble, and when the people dug one out, it rang again, and to him it sounded like a promise that the city would live.
Nagai also spoke of the bombing in religious terms, as a sacrifice, and other survivors and writers have strongly disagreed with that. His words comforted some and troubled others.
Harder to argue with is what he did with his hands. He grieved and he worked, both at once. Jesus said, in Matthew: "Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted."
Nagai didn't wait to be comforted before he started caring for others.

how: In Nagasaki, Nagai's hut is preserved beside a memorial museum, and Catholics in the Urakami community remember the bombing each August with Mass and prayer for peace at the rebuilt cathedral.

games.q: you're a doctor, wounded yourself, in a city that has just been destroyed. your home and family are across town. what do you do first?
o: go home at once to find your wife.
treat the wounded in front of you.
leave the city to get help for your own wounds.
games.why: Nagai set up first aid in the ruins and worked until he collapsed. only then did he go home, and found his wife's remains and her rosary.

practice: If you're carrying a loss right now, a person, a place, a plan, name it without hurrying it away; if not, bring to mind someone who is.

Then notice who near you might need something, and one small act of care you could offer, not instead of grieving but alongside it. If you pray, say the line from Matthew: blessed are they that mourn.
